source.title: Association of Acceleration with Spatiotemporal Variables in Maximal Sprinting

paper.citation: Nagahara, R., Naito, H., Morin, J.-B., & Zushi, K. (2014). Association of acceleration with spatiotemporal variables in maximal sprinting. International Journal of Sports Medicine, 35(9), 755–761. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0033-1363252
paper.abstract: How is step-to-step acceleration associated with changes in step length, step frequency, support time, and flight time? Twenty-one healthy male university sprinters, age 20.1 ± 1.2 years, 100-m best 10.72–11.80 s. One maximal 60-m sprint from blocks on a track. Sprint-specialist context; transfer to collegiate American-football starts and curved/reactive sprints is indirect. Cross-sectional biomechanical analysis using six 300-Hz panning cameras. Foot strike/toe-off and toe coordinates were used to derive step-level variables and their rates of change. Correlations were calculated at each step without a reported correction for the large number of repeated tests.
paper.tldr: This study informs phase-specific interpretation of step length and frequency during maximal acceleration. Acceleration correlated with step-length rate of change at steps 5–19 (r = 0.45–0.72). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional biomechanical analysis using six 300-Hz panning cameras. Foot strike/toe-off and toe coordinates were used to derive step-level variables and their rates of change. Correlations were calculated at each step without a reported correction for the large number of repeated tests.
paper.findings: Acceleration correlated with step-length rate of change at steps 5–19 (r = 0.45–0.72). Acceleration correlated with step-frequency rate of change in the first two steps (r = 0.51–0.63) and last three analyzed steps (r = 0.44–0.47). Step-length and step-frequency rates of change were negatively correlated at every step (r = -0.83 to -0.55), showing a coordination tradeoff rather than independent levers.
paper.limitations: Each athlete completed only one analyzed sprint. Step number standardized athletes who reached the same step at different times and distances, introducing alignment bias. Small male sprint sample and multiple stepwise correlations limit precision and increase false-positive risk. Associations do not show that externally forcing step length or frequency will improve acceleration; the authors caution that manipulation can impair performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Use step length and frequency as descriptive outputs of an athlete's acceleration strategy, not isolated technique targets. Diagnose phases alongside force application and posture, and verify that any cue improves sprint time rather than simply changing a correlated variable.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use step length and frequency as descriptive outputs of an athlete's acceleration strategy, not isolated technique targets. Diagnose phases alongside force application and posture, and verify that any cue improves sprint time rather than simply changing a correlated variable. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
